summary: The Network Service Header is added to packets or frames to realize Service Function Paths. It also allows metadata to be exchanged along those paths. NSH is the encapsulation needed for the service function chaining architecture.

plainLanguage.summary: The Network Service Header (NSH) adds information that directs a packet through a sequence of network services. It can also carry details that those services use when handling the packet.

questions: what is the network service header
what is the nsh service index
how does nsh service function chaining work
subtitle: A header that carries a service path, its current position, and optional information between network services.

tldr.problem: A network needs to steer packets through chosen service functions without tying those functions to fixed network locations.
tldr.mechanism: A classifier adds an NSH with a path identifier, a service index, and optional context. Service Function Forwarders use the path fields to select the next service, while an outer transport carries the packet.
tldr.outcome: RFC 8300 defines the encapsulation required by the Service Function Chaining architecture. It is a Proposed Standard updated by RFC 9451.

today: RFC 8300 is a Proposed Standard updated by RFC 9451; it has not been obsoleted. It defines the NSH encapsulation for the Service Function Chaining architecture.

sections.title: The Service-Path Header
sections.content:
RFC 8300 specifies the Network Service Header (NSH), an encapsulation for Service Function Chaining. A classifier adds it to an original packet or frame, and an outer transport encapsulation carries the result to NSH-aware network elements.

The NSH identifies a Service Function Path, indicates a position within that path, and can carry per-packet metadata. Its intended scope is one provider's operational domain; an NSH-aware control plane is outside this RFC's scope.
sections.plainLanguage: The NSH tells participating network nodes which service path a packet follows and where it is on that path. It may also carry information that services along the path need.

sections.title: The NSH Header Layout
sections.content:
The NSH begins with a 4-byte Base Header and a 4-byte Service Path Header. Optional Context Headers follow them. The Base Header identifies the format and payload protocol; the Service Path Header identifies the path and the position within it.

The Base Header's length is measured in 4-byte words. MD Type 0x1 requires a 16-byte context header. MD Type 0x2 permits zero or more variable-length context headers, whose data is padded to a 4-byte boundary.
sections.plainLanguage: The NSH starts with two fixed headers that identify the path and its payload. Optional context headers can follow and carry additional information.

sections.title: The Base Header Fields
sections.content:
The Base Header is one 32-bit word. It contains a version, an OAM flag, a TTL, a length, an MD Type, and a Next Protocol value. In this revision, senders set the version to 0x0; the Next Protocol value identifies the encapsulated data, which the NSH does not change.

The TTL limits Service Function Forwarder hops and is the primary loop-prevention mechanism. Each forwarder decrements it before lookup, and must not forward a packet if the resulting value is zero. If no initial TTL is configured, the default is 63.
sections.plainLanguage: The Base Header identifies the NSH format, its size, and the type of data inside it. Forwarders reduce its hop limit so a packet cannot circulate through the service network indefinitely.

sections.title: Selecting the Next Service
sections.content:
The Service Path Header contains a 24-bit Service Path Identifier (SPI) and an 8-bit Service Index (SI). The SPI identifies the path; the SI marks the packet's position in it. The initial classifier should set the SI to 255 unless the control plane configures another value.

Service Functions and SFC Proxies decrement the SI after doing their work. A Service Function Forwarder uses the SPI and SI together to select the next service and the network locator used to reach it. An SFF that is not the terminal forwarder drops a packet with SI zero.
sections.plainLanguage: The path identifier names the service path, while the service index marks the packet's place in it. Service functions reduce that index, and forwarders use both values to choose the next destination.

sections.title: What NSH-Aware Nodes Do
sections.content:
A classifier inserts an NSH at the start of a service path. Service Function Forwarders select the next service, and Service Functions decrement the service index after processing. The last forwarder removes the NSH before sending the original packet onward.

A classifier may change the path by replacing the NSH after reclassification. A proxy can remove the NSH before passing a packet to a service that does not understand it, then add it back with the service index decremented. Services can also use NSH metadata when selecting or enforcing policy.
sections.plainLanguage: The classifier starts the path, forwarders direct packets, and services update the path position after processing. The final forwarder removes the NSH before the packet leaves the service path.

sections.title: Transport and Packet Size
sections.content:
The NSH is independent of the outer transport encapsulation. Transit network nodes forward that outer encapsulation without changing the NSH. Adding both headers increases packet size, so an operator can provide enough underlay MTU to avoid fragmentation within the managed domain.

The NSH itself does not define fragmentation. Any required fragmentation belongs to the transport encapsulation; when IP carries NSH, the RFC points to IP fragmentation and Path MTU Discovery. Fragmentation must not duplicate the NSH header.
sections.plainLanguage: An outer transport carries the packet and NSH between service nodes. If the added headers make a packet too large, the transport layer handles fragmentation, not the NSH.

sections.title: Trust and Security Boundaries
sections.content:
NSH is not an end-to-end protocol. Network devices add it at the service-domain entrance and remove it at the exit, so the design assumes that the operator trusts and maintains the classifiers, forwarders, and service functions inside that domain.

Domain edges must filter the transport encapsulation and reject packets carrying an NSH from outside or leaving with one. NSH does not require its own integrity protection. If an operator decides protection is necessary, the outer transport must provide it; sensitive metadata should be limited to what the path needs, and subscriber identifiers should generally be obscured.
sections.plainLanguage: NSH is intended to stay inside one trusted network domain. Edge devices remove or reject it, and operators must protect sensitive metadata when their risk assessment requires protection.

fields.desc: Version 0x0 is used in this revision.

fields.name: TTL
fields.desc: Limits Service Function Forwarder hops; default initial value is 63.
